Opinion: Mom and Dad, I’m not a child anymore

Apparently, leaving the nest doesn’t fly with everybody
Abby Morris, Opinion Writer
September 28, 2026
Photo by Susana Lazcano
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:58
Instaread

Parenting is hard, but being an adult with parents who still see you as a child might be harder. There’s nothing worse than having proved you’re a capable, responsible adult and still having your parents treat you like a child. Yet, this is a common problem young adults today face, and instead of our parents pushing us out of the nest, we’re now having to force our way out.

I have personally struggled with this and understand how challenging it can be to navigate this new dynamic because I love my parents — they provided me with a great life, and I’m incredibly grateful to them for all of their love and support — but it took a long time for them to let go and finally see me as an adult. It didn’t matter that I was 21 years old with great grades and two out-of-state internships; it still felt like I was in high school and having to ask for permission or be worried about getting in trouble.

To a degree, I understand. We’re all used to a certain way of life after having spent 18 years under one roof together where we were dependent on them and had to follow their rules. But expecting this dynamic to continue throughout college is harmful and, unfortunately, the reality for younger generations. Instead of allowing their children to become independent, many parents continue to hold on. This has shifted college from a place to be free of parental oversight to an extension of high school. 

For some parents, it’s about not having control over their child’s actions. For others, it’s excessively worrying about potential danger. Take, for example, college parent Facebook groups, where posts range from “How do I make sure my daughter doesn’t have boys in her dorm?” and “Where can I get a list of professors’ emails to establish a line of communication?” to “How do I ask the college to install cameras in my child’s dorm room?” These posts might seem like the innocent anxieties or old habits of a parent, but they’re really just blatant proof that parents today are too involved.

There’s always going to be the parent-child dynamic and, sometimes, there will be moments when you need your Mom and Dad’s help. That’s okay. But this unhealthy dynamic is far from that I am referring to. Research has shown that helicopter parenting has negative outcomes such as poor coping skills, inadequate life skills and low self-esteem and self-image. Additionally, being too strict or overprotective is more likely to make your child lie to you or feel like they can’t tell you anything.

Parents need to realize it’s no longer their responsibility to remind their adult children of deadlines or tell them what they’re “supposed” to do. That’s what the past 18 years were for, and at some point, they’re going to have to trust that all those years of parenting taught their child right from wrong. 

We cannot become functioning adults after college if our parents still hold us on a leash. College is the time to make mistakes and learn from them — it’s still a relatively safe and protected environment. Yes, these mistakes might make our parents mad. Some might even significantly alter your life, but isn’t that part of growing up? If we don’t have the freedom to live, will we go through life afraid of making mistakes, not knowing how to do things on our own or how to form healthy relationships? I truly doubt this is what parents want for their children. 

No parent wants to let their kid go, but it’s a crucial part of life. Being overprotective and babying adult children won’t help; it’ll only create resentment. 

So, on behalf of the adult children struggling with this, I say to the parents, “Let us go.”

Abby Morris is an English honors and political science senior and opinion writer for The Battalion.
